title: Telling a story
hookLine: Esther tells the king in Mordecai's name, and the name saves him; say where a story came from
tomorrow: who told the Buddha's own son to practice the breath?
last: A GOOD DAY · THE EVENING · GOODNIGHT

cards: A story is going around the group chat: a screenshot of a screenshot, and nobody knows who said it first. The book of Esther cares a great deal about who said it first.
Mordecai, sitting at the king's gate, learns that two of the king's doorkeepers are plotting to kill him. He tells Esther, his cousin, who is now the queen.
And she passes it on like this: "and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai's name." The plot fails. It's written down in the king's chronicles, and nobody thanks Mordecai.
Then, one night, the king can't sleep.

teach.b: So he has the chronicles read to him, and there it is: Mordecai saved the king, and nothing was ever done for him.
That sleepless night turns the whole story, at the very moment Mordecai's enemy Haman has come to ask for his death.
Mordecai's name saved him, and it was there because Esther said where the warning came from. The rabbis built a teaching on that one line.

teach.h: AVOT: IN THE NAME OF WHO SAID IT.
teach.b: Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, says whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it brings redemption into the world, and it gives Esther as the proof.
It's a living Jewish habit, and you can see it on the Talmud's pages, in chains like: this rabbi said, in the name of that rabbi. A story handed on with its source keeps its teller alive in it.

teach.h: THE SOURCE IS PART OF THE GIFT.
teach.b: So when you pass on a story from this path, Honi's carob tree or Yunmen's good day, the first line is part of the gift: this comes from the Talmud.
This one's from a Zen collection.

how: Jewish study passes teachings on with their chain of names, following Pirkei Avot's line about saying a thing in its teller's name; people who borrow it start a story by naming where it came from.

o: passing on a story along with where it came from
making a story up to fit the person listening

games.q: the name that saved him: tap the pairs.
p: overheard the plot at the king's gate
told the king in Mordecai's name
had the chronicles read to him

s: Esther told the king the warning came from her
she spoke 'in Mordecai's name', and that line became a Jewish teaching.
naming a story's source is just politeness
the popular view. Pirkei Avot says it brings redemption into the world, and gives Esther as proof.
Mordecai's good deed went unrewarded until the king couldn't sleep
the chronicles were read to him, and he learned nothing had been done for Mordecai.

games.q: you're telling your nephew a story you heard on a podcast, about a monk and a teacup. you don't know where it began. what fits the Esther teaching?
o: say what you know: 'i heard it on a podcast; i'm not sure where it began.'
call it a Zen story; that's probably where it's from anyway.
tell it as your own; where it's from doesn't change the lesson.
games.why: Avot asks you to say a thing in the name of the one who said it. when you don't know the name, saying so keeps the chain honest.

practice: Choose one story from this path you could tell in a minute: the carob planter, the sheep, the spice box. Tell it to yourself, quietly, out loud, and start with its home: in the Talmud, there's a man planting a tree.

wordCard.voice: Telling a story: handing it on with its source, so the one who first told it travels with it.

orig.note: Hebrew: in the name of the one who said it, the phrase from Pirkei Avot 6:6.

carryVoice: The line for today: say where it came from, the way Esther spoke in Mordecai's name. That's the week.

sources.q: and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai's name.

sources.ref: Esther 2:21-23; 6:1-4 (the plot, the chronicles, the sleepless night, 'there is nothing done for him', Haman arriving)
Pirkei Avot 6:6 (whoever says a thing in the name of the one who said it brings redemption into the world, citing Esther 2:22); also Talmud Megillah 15a
